posts.title: Welcome to PeptideSuppliers.org: How to Find a Peptide Supplier for Your Research Needs
posts.h1: Welcome to PeptideSuppliers.org: how to find a peptide supplier for your research needs
posts.description: What PeptideSuppliers.org is, how the supplier database works, how we rate suppliers, and a short checklist for choosing a research peptide supplier.
posts.body:
PeptideSuppliers.org is a searchable database of research peptide suppliers. The idea is simple: if you know what you need, you should be able to see who sells it, what documentation they publish, how they ship, and how you can pay, without opening twenty tabs.

Why we built it

Looking for a research peptide supplier usually means sorting through storefronts that all say the same things: “third-party tested,” “high purity,” “fast shipping.” Very few show you the evidence. Some publish a certificate of analysis (COA) for every lot; others show a single sample report, or nothing until you ask. Payment options range from ordinary cards to peer-to-peer apps and crypto that are hard to reverse if something goes wrong.

We wanted one place that puts those differences side by side. Right now the database covers {n} suppliers, and every one has its own review page with the details we could verify.

How to use the database

Start at the supplier database and search by supplier or compound. Then narrow the list with filters:

  • Compound: show only suppliers that list the material you are looking for, such as BPC-157, GHK-Cu, or tesamorelin.
  • COA status: separate suppliers that publish COAs from those that offer them on request or show only testing language.
  • Price tier and shipping: filter by budget, mid-range, or premium, and by whether a supplier ships outside the US.
  • Country and payment: find US or UK suppliers, and see which payment methods each accepts.
  • Ordered by us: show suppliers where we placed an order and received product.

Every card links to a full review, so you can see why a supplier looks the way it does before you click through to its site.

How we rate suppliers

Our ratings are about documentation, clarity, and buyer risk, not about product quality. We do not run our own lab tests, so we do not claim to know that any vial contains what its label says. What we can check is what a buyer can check: whether COAs exist and name a lab, whether a report is tied to a specific lot, whether policies and prices are published, and how recourse works if an order goes wrong. Our methodology page explains the approach in more detail.

Where we have ordered, we say so on the listing and write up what arrived. Where we have not, the review is based on the supplier’s public pages, and it says that too.

How the site is funded

We are upfront about this because it matters. Some suppliers pay for a featured, clearly labeled “Sponsored” placement, and some links include referral or discount codes that can earn us a commission. Those links are marked as sponsored, and a sponsored listing does not change a supplier’s rating. The full policy is on our disclosure page. If you run a supplier and want to be featured, see the contact page.

A short checklist for choosing a supplier

  1. Start with the exact material and form you need, then check which suppliers list it.
  2. Look for a COA that names the lab, the methods, and the lot, and ask whether the report covers the lot that will be shipped.
  3. Check what the report does and does not show. Purity, identity, and content are different measurements.
  4. Compare the delivered price, not just the sticker price: shipping, tax, bundle discounts, and minimums all change the total.
  5. Look at payment methods. Cards offer dispute options; bank transfers, crypto, and peer-to-peer apps usually do not.
  6. Read the refund and damage policy before you order, not after.

What this site is not

Everything we list is sold for laboratory research use only. We do not give dosing, administration, or medical advice, and nothing on this site is intended for human or veterinary use. See our medical disclaimer. Laws on buying and importing these materials differ by country, so check the rules where you are before ordering.

What is coming next

We will keep adding suppliers, keep updating reviews as policies and prices change, and place more orders so we can report on what actually arrives. We will also publish short guides on reading COAs, comparing delivered quotes, and spotting red flags. If a supplier is missing, a detail is wrong, or you have a good or bad experience to report, tell us.

posts.title: Tesamorelin Explained: What It Is, How It Is Studied, and How to Evaluate Suppliers
posts.h1: Tesamorelin explained: what it is, how it is studied, and how to evaluate suppliers
posts.description: A research-use-only guide to tesamorelin: its structure, why the N-terminal change matters, how it is studied, what a good batch record shows, and how to compare suppliers.
posts.body:
Tesamorelin is one of the most studied growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) analogs, and it is also one of the easiest peptides to misunderstand. It is a prescription drug in one form and a laboratory research chemical in another. This guide explains what the compound is, how it is studied, what separates a well-documented research batch from a poorly documented one, and how to evaluate suppliers that list it.

Everything on PeptideSuppliers.org is about laboratory research materials. This article does not give dosing, administration, or medical advice, and nothing here is intended for human or veterinary use. See our medical disclaimer.

What tesamorelin is

Tesamorelin is a synthetic analog of human growth hormone-releasing hormone, the 44-amino-acid hypothalamic peptide that signals the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. Its sequence follows the full length of human GHRH(1–44), with one deliberate change: a trans-3-hexenoyl group is attached to the N-terminus of the peptide. Its molecular weight is roughly 5.1 kDa, which makes it a much larger molecule than short research peptides such as BPC-157 (15 amino acids) or KPV (3 amino acids).

That size matters for anyone sourcing it. Longer peptides are harder to synthesize and purify, they are more prone to truncated or modified by-products, and their analytical profile is more complicated. A purity figure that looks excellent for a 15-residue peptide can mean something different for a 44-residue one, which is why the documentation questions later in this article are especially important for tesamorelin.

Why the N-terminal modification exists

Natural GHRH is cleared from the body very quickly. A major reason is an enzyme called dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4), which cleaves two amino acids from the N-terminus and inactivates the hormone within minutes. The trans-3-hexenoyl group on tesamorelin was introduced to make the molecule more resistant to that cleavage, so that the intact peptide persists long enough to be studied and used as a reference compound.

This is the main reason tesamorelin is described as a “stabilized” GHRH analog. The core sequence is still the one the GHRH receptor recognizes; the change is at the end that DPP-4 attacks. It also explains why tesamorelin is often compared with CJC-1295 without DAC, a shorter GHRH analog (a modified 29-amino-acid fragment) that is built differently and behaves differently in assays.

How it is studied in the laboratory

Tesamorelin acts at the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotroph cells. In research settings the receptor engagement leads to cyclic AMP signaling and the release of growth hormone, which in turn drives downstream insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) production in the liver and other tissues. Because tesamorelin acts upstream of growth hormone and not by supplying growth hormone itself, it is used to study how the GH axis responds to receptor stimulation, including the pulsatile pattern of GH release.

Typical research questions include:

  • Receptor pharmacology: binding, signaling, and desensitization at the GHRH receptor in cell-based assays.
  • Pituitary models: how somatotroph cells or pituitary tissue respond to GHRH analogs compared with other secretagogues.
  • GH/IGF-1 axis biology: how stimulation upstream changes IGF-1 and related markers in experimental systems.
  • Metabolic and lipid-marker work: how GH-axis signaling relates to fat metabolism and lipid markers in published models.
  • Comparative studies: head-to-head work with other GHRH analogs and with ghrelin-receptor agonists such as ipamorelin.

Reference compounds are valuable only when their identity and quality are known. A receptor study run with an under-dosed, degraded, or mislabeled batch can produce results that look like biology but are really chemistry. That is the argument for treating documentation as seriously as price.

Regulatory context: a drug and a research chemical

Tesamorelin is also an approved medicine. In 2010 the US Food and Drug Administration approved a tesamorelin product for a specific clinical indication in adults with HIV-associated lipodystrophy. We mention this for context, not as guidance: it is the reason tesamorelin has an unusually deep body of published clinical literature compared with most peptides in our database.

It is also the source of confusion. The approved medicine is a manufactured, regulated, prescription product with defined manufacturing standards. The tesamorelin sold by research suppliers is a different thing: a laboratory material sold for research use only, with whatever quality its manufacturer and tester can document. The two should not be treated as interchangeable, and research suppliers state that their materials are not for human or veterinary use. Laws on buying, possessing, and importing these materials differ by country, so check the rules where you are before ordering.

What a good tesamorelin batch record should show

Because tesamorelin is a large peptide, the questions below matter more than they do for short peptides. Our introduction to the site describes our general approach; here is how it applies to this compound.

  1. Identity by mass spectrometry. HPLC retention time alone does not prove the molecule is tesamorelin. A mass-spec result confirming the expected molecular weight (about 5.1 kDa) is the stronger identity check. Ask which method the report used.
  2. Purity by HPLC, with the method stated. A purity percentage is only as meaningful as the method behind it. Look for the wavelength, the gradient or column details if provided, and the date. For a 44-residue peptide, a figure in the high 90s is common, but the report should show the chromatogram or at least name the method.
  3. Content versus label. A vial labeled 10 mg may not contain 10 mg of peptide. Lyophilized peptides include counterions and residual water, so measured content can differ from the nominal amount. A report that states the measured quantity against the label is more informative than one that only gives purity.
  4. Endotoxin and sterility, if claimed. If a supplier says the material is tested for endotoxin or sterility, the report should say so, with the method and the specification. Not every report includes every assay, and purity does not prove sterility.
  5. Lot linkage. The report should name a batch or lot number that matches the vial you receive, plus the laboratory, the date, and ideally a way to verify it with the lab itself. A single report for a different lot is evidence about that lot only.

A report that covers these points is not a guarantee, because it describes the sample tested. But it is far better than a general “third-party tested” badge, and it makes mistakes and inconsistencies easier to spot.

Handling notes from the research literature

Suppliers and researchers describe a few practical issues with tesamorelin in the laboratory. These are general handling points, not usage instructions:

  • Storage of lyophilized material. Most suppliers specify cold, dark, dry storage of the sealed lyophilized powder and warn against repeated freeze–thaw cycles once the material is in solution. Follow the storage conditions printed on the certificate and the label.
  • Solubility and gelling. Because it is a long peptide, tesamorelin can be slow to dissolve and may form gels or clumps under some conditions. At least one supplier publishes a technical note on tesamorelin gelling, which tells you the issue is common enough to document. Check solubility data for your own protocol before planning work.
  • Counterion and salt form. The salt form (often an acetate) affects the mass-to-peptide ratio and solubility. If a report does not say how content was measured, ask.
  • Documentation after opening. Record the lot number, date, and storage history of every vial. Stock that cannot be traced to a certificate is hard to troubleshoot when results look odd.

Comparing tesamorelin with related compounds

Researchers often compare tesamorelin with other GH-axis tools. A short orientation:

  • CJC-1295 (no DAC): a shorter GHRH analog with several amino-acid substitutions. It acts at the same receptor, but it is a different molecule with different stability and analytical behavior.
  • Ipamorelin: a growth hormone secretagogue that acts at the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R), a different pathway from GHRH analogs. It is frequently studied alongside GHRH analogs, and blends of CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are common in supplier catalogs.
  • Sermorelin: a shorter GHRH fragment (the first 29 residues) that is the older, simpler relative of these analogs.

Choosing among them is a question of the experimental design, not of which is “stronger.” We bring them up because suppliers sometimes group them together on a single page, and their documentation needs are not identical. A report for a blend should show how each component was measured.

Using the database to find a tesamorelin supplier

If you are looking for tesamorelin, the quickest route is the supplier database filtered to tesamorelin. From there you can narrow by published COA status, price tier, country, and shipping. Each result links to a full review so you can see what we could and could not verify.

As an illustration of why the documentation filter matters, here is how three suppliers in the database present tesamorelin as of late October 2026. Prices are for a 10 mg vial and change often:

  • Aurelia Research lists tesamorelin with a batch-level certificate (purity reported at 99.60% for the batch in its library) and a lookup page that names the laboratory and test date. It is a new company, so we note its short history. US listing was about $84.99.
  • Disguised Alpha lists tesamorelin in 5, 10, and 20 mg sizes (10 mg about $79.99) and has a large COA portal, though we flag that its testing and payment claims differ between pages.
  • Ageless Peptides lists tesamorelin 10 mg at about $89.99 with bundle pricing, but we found no visible lab report on that product page.
Sponsored

Iron Peptides: tesamorelin 10 mg

Iron Peptides is a sponsored supplier on this site and lists a 10 mg tesamorelin product. Use code IRONMAN for 10% off. We placed our own order with Iron Peptides for a different product, which we describe in its review; we have not ordered or tested this tesamorelin. When we checked, the store sent visitors to a sign-in page before showing the product, so confirm the batch report and price once you are in.

Sponsored link. We earn a commission and a fee for placement, which does not change our ratings. See our disclosure.

View at Iron Peptides

Prices alone would rank these differently than documentation does. That is the point: with a 44-residue peptide, a low price with no batch record is a bigger gamble than a modest premium with a verifiable report. We rate documentation and buyer risk, not product quality, because we do not run our own assays, and we say on each review whether we have ordered.

A short checklist before you order tesamorelin

  1. Confirm the exact material, strength, and salt form you need.
  2. Find a batch-specific report that names the lab, the method, and the lot, and verify it with the lab if a link is offered.
  3. Check that identity was confirmed by mass spectrometry, and that content is reported against the label.
  4. Compare delivered price, including shipping, bundles, and any minimum order.
  5. Look at payment options and the refund policy before you fill the basket. Card payments allow disputes; bank transfers, crypto, and peer-to-peer apps usually do not.
  6. Check the laws that apply to you for purchase, possession, and import.

The bottom line

Tesamorelin is a well-characterized GHRH analog with a long research history, a modified 44-residue structure, and an unusual dual identity as both a regulated medicine and a research chemical. For a laboratory buyer, the right questions are about identity, purity, content, and traceability, not marketing language. Use the database filter, read the batch record, and keep your own records. If a supplier is missing, a detail is out of date, or you have a documented experience to share, tell us.

posts.title: Tirzepatide: The Latest Research and the Hype Around It (2026)
posts.h1: Tirzepatide: what the latest research shows, and where the hype outruns the evidence
posts.description: A plain-language look at tirzepatide in 2026: SURMOUNT-5, SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN, cardiovascular data, a new brown-fat mouse study, and the FDA's warnings about unapproved versions.
posts.body:
Few drugs have moved from the medical literature to everyday conversation as fast as tirzepatide. It is sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, it keeps producing headline-sized trial results, and it has also become a magnet for grey-market sales. This guide separates what the published research actually shows from the hype around it, using primary sources wherever we could. It is information for readers, not medical advice.

Editorial note: tirzepatide is an FDA-approved prescription medicine. This site is a directory of research-peptide suppliers, and nothing here is dosing, sourcing or treatment guidance. Where we cite figures, the source is linked at the end. We have not tested any product.

What tirzepatide is

Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid synthetic peptide built on the sequence of GIP, the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, and modified so that it activates two receptors at once: the GIP receptor and the GLP-1 receptor. That dual action is the central idea. Semaglutide, the other household name in this class, activates only the GLP-1 receptor. Tirzepatide is also attached to a fatty-acid side chain that lets it bind albumin in the blood, which is what allows a once-weekly injection.

It is approved in the United States under two brand names: Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and Zepbound for chronic weight management, and Zepbound also carries an approval for moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Those are pharmaceutical products, made under regulatory controls, prescribed by clinicians, and supported by large randomized trials. That regulatory status matters for everything that follows.

The headline result: tirzepatide versus semaglutide

The comparison that drove most of the attention is SURMOUNT-5, a head-to-head, open-label trial in about 750 adults with obesity or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, it reported average weight loss of 20.2% with tirzepatide against 13.7% with semaglutide at 72 weeks, a difference of 6.5 percentage points. In kilograms that was roughly 22.8 versus 15.0. Waist circumference fell by about 18 cm on tirzepatide and 13 cm on semaglutide. Side effects were mainly gastrointestinal, consistent with earlier trials.

Two cautions are worth holding onto. First, those are average results at the highest tolerated doses, not a prediction for any individual. Second, the design was open-label, meaning participants and investigators knew which drug was being used, which is normal for a trial comparing two injectables but is a limitation. The result is genuinely strong evidence that tirzepatide produces larger average weight loss than semaglutide in this setting. It does not tell you what any one person will experience.

The newest big study: keeping weight off

The most recent major trial result is SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN, published in The Lancet in May 2026, and it asks a question people care about: what happens when treatment is reduced or stopped? The trial enrolled 441 US adults with obesity in a 60-week open-label weight-loss phase. Of those, 378 who had lost at least 5% of their body weight and tolerated at least 10 mg were then randomized into a 52-week double-blind maintenance phase: continue at their maximum tolerated dose, drop to a 5 mg dose, or switch to placebo.

At 112 weeks, average weight change from the start of the trial was minus 21.9% for those who continued the maximum tolerated dose, minus 16.6% for the 5 mg group and minus 9.9% for placebo. Only 8% of the maximum-dose group and 25% of the 5 mg group regained at least half of their lost weight, compared with 67% of the placebo group. Participants who regained more than half of their loss could receive rescue tirzepatide, so the placebo figure understates how much weight might be regained with no further treatment. The takeaway reported by the investigators and an accompanying editorial is that continued therapy matters for long-term management, and that a reduced dose retained a good share of the benefit. Adverse events were more common with tirzepatide than placebo, mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal effects.

Beyond weight: the heart

Weight is only part of the story, and cardiovascular outcomes are where the most consequential data sit. SURPASS-CVOT compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide, an older GLP-1 drug with proven cardiovascular benefit, in people with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2025, it met its prespecified goal of non-inferiority for major adverse cardiovascular events, with a hazard ratio of about 0.92 and a confidence interval (0.83 to 1.01) that just crossed 1.0. In plain terms, tirzepatide was shown to be at least as protective as dulaglutide, with a numerical edge that was not statistically conclusive. A lower rate of death from any cause was reported, but that was an exploratory finding and should not be over-read.

It is also important to know what this is not. It is not a trial against placebo, so it does not directly measure how much cardiovascular risk tirzepatide removes compared with no treatment. Analyses that try to estimate that by indirect comparison exist, but they are exactly that: estimates.

Early-stage science: brown fat in mice

Some of the newest headlines are about mechanism. In September 2026, researchers at the University of Barcelona reported in the journal Biomedicine and Pharmacotherapy that tirzepatide activated brown adipose tissue, the calorie-burning type of fat, in obese mice. Crucially, they compared the treated animals with untreated mice given the same amount of food, which let them separate effects of the drug from effects of eating less. The finding suggests tirzepatide may influence energy expenditure in addition to suppressing appetite.

The authors themselves are careful: this is a mouse study, and mouse and human metabolism, and fat distribution, differ substantially. Brown fat is also less abundant in adult humans. It is a hypothesis-generating result, a reason for further human research, and not evidence that the drug does the same thing in people. Treat articles that present it as established fact with suspicion.

Where the hype outruns the evidence

Three patterns recur whenever a drug becomes this famous.

Dose and speed folklore. Online communities trade ideas about higher doses, faster escalation, and unusual regimens. The evidence base is the approved regimens used in the trials. The FDA has said it received reports of adverse events that may relate to patients using compounded semaglutide or tirzepatide products at doses beyond those in the approved label, including more product per dose, more frequent doses, or faster escalation. Some of the events were serious.

Surrogate-endpoint enthusiasm. Every new mechanistic paper, in mice or in a post-hoc analysis, is quickly framed as a new benefit. Post-hoc subgroup analyses and observational cohort studies are useful for generating questions, but they are weaker than randomized trials, and they are frequently reported without those caveats.

Equating every product with the approved drug. This is the most consequential one, and it brings us to the market around the drug.

The grey market: what the FDA says

Because demand has outstripped supply for long stretches, a large market has grown up in compounded versions and in products labeled for laboratory use. The FDA maintains a page on unapproved GLP-1 drugs, last updated October 1, 2026, and it is unusually direct. It says compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and the agency does not review them for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed, and that compounded drugs should only be used in patients whose medical needs cannot be met by an approved drug.

It also describes problems it has seen: fraudulent products whose labels name pharmacies that do not exist, dosing errors resulting from patients measuring doses themselves, injectable products that arrived warm without enough ice packs, and concerns about multi-dose vials used beyond 28 days. As of May 31, 2026, the agency had received more than 730 adverse-event reports associated with compounded tirzepatide, with the caveat that it is not always possible to tell whether a drug caused an event, and that underreporting is likely because many compounders are not required to report.

Most relevant to a site like this one, the FDA states that it has warned companies selling unapproved drugs containing semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide, survodutide or mazdutide that are falsely labeled "for research purposes" or "not for human consumption," when those products are being sold directly to consumers for human use with dosing instructions. It urges consumers not to purchase them, describing them as of unknown quality and potentially harmful. The agency also states that retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law.

Our position, stated plainly

PeptideSuppliers.org lists suppliers of research peptides and reviews their public documentation. We do not endorse any product for human use, we do not give dosing guidance, and we do not treat a certificate of analysis as a substitute for regulatory oversight. A COA is a lab report about one sample from one batch. It cannot establish sterility, safety, or suitability for injection, and for a drug as widely used as tirzepatide, an approved product dispensed through a licensed pharmacy is a different thing altogether from a vial sold as a research chemical.

Some suppliers in our database list tirzepatide or related compounds in their catalogs. Where we mention them, we are reporting what they sell, not recommending it. If you are considering any GLP-1 or GIP medication for a health reason, the right conversation is with a licensed clinician, and the right source is a state-licensed pharmacy, as the FDA advises. If you are a researcher working with these compounds in vitro or in animals, the documentation checks we describe elsewhere on the site apply, along with your institution's rules and the law where you are.

What to watch next

The research pipeline is moving quickly, and several things are worth following: further analyses from SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN on lower-dose strategies; long-term outcome trials in heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease; human studies on whether the brown-fat finding translates; and the growing list of competing and next-generation agents, from triple agonists to oral drugs. The honest summary today is that tirzepatide has some of the strongest randomized evidence of any weight-management drug, that it is a prescription medicine with real side effects, and that much of what circulates online about it, especially around unapproved versions, goes well beyond what the evidence supports.

Sources

  • FDA, FDA’s Concerns with Unapproved GLP-1 Drugs Used for Weight Loss (content current as of October 1, 2026)
  • American College of Cardiology, SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN: Continuing Tirzepatide Maintains Weight Loss (May 18, 2026), summarizing Horn et al., The Lancet, 2026
  • ScienceDaily / University of Barcelona, Zepbound and Mounjaro may turn on the body’s calorie-burning brown fat (September 26, 2026)
  • Aronne et al., SURMOUNT-5, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025 (doi 10.1056/NEJMoa2416394)
  • Nicholls et al., SURPASS-CVOT, New England Journal of Medicine, 2025;393:2409-2420
